teile.einleitung: The canine teeth are the pointed teeth at the corner of the dental arch. They stand right next to the incisors and help with holding and tearing food.
wichtigste: The canine teeth stand next to the incisors.
In the permanent set of teeth there are four canines, two at the top and two at the bottom.
Canine teeth are pointed.
You use them for holding and tearing.
The upper canine has the longest root of all teeth.
The upper canines are also known as eye teeth in everyday language.

abschnitte.text: At the front of the mouth are the **incisors**. Right next to them, at the **corner of the dental arch**, come the **canines**. There are two at the top and two at the bottom, so **four** altogether. Behind them come the molars. Children's **milk teeth** also already include four canines.

A canine tapers to a **point** at the top. With it you can **hold** and **tear** tough food well, for example a piece of bread crust. The incisors bite off, and the molars grind the food. So each type of tooth has its own job.

The **upper canine** has the **longest root** of all human teeth. That is why it sits very firmly in the jaw. Its root reaches far up towards the eye. That is why the upper canines are also called **eye teeth** in everyday language. Because they are so sturdy, they often stay in place into old age.

Many **predators** have very large, long canines. The **tiger** uses them to seize its prey. In **dogs** and **wolves**, the long canines are called **fangs**. In some animals, canines have grown into huge tusks, for example in the walrus or the wild boar.

gewusst: An adult's permanent set of teeth has 32 teeth including the wisdom teeth, and the milk teeth have 20.
The tusks of elephants are not canines but greatly elongated incisors.

teile.einleitung: An electron microscope magnifies tiny things much more strongly than a light microscope. Instead of light, it uses a beam of electrons.
wichtigste: Ernst Ruska built the first electron microscope with Max Knoll from 1931.
Ruska received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1986.
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, which gives higher resolution.
Inside the machine there is a high vacuum, so that air does not scatter the electrons.
Magnetic fields from coils focus the electron beam.
The Swiss scientist Jacques Dubochet received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017 for cryo-electron microscopy.

abschnitte.text: How finely a microscope shows details depends on the **wavelength**. Light microscopes reach a limit of about 200 nanometres. Fast **electrons** have a wavelength of only a few picometres. That is why the **resolution** is much higher. This makes it possible, for example, to see **ribosomes**, which measure only 20 to 30 nanometres.

Inside the machine there has to be a **high vacuum**, because even a few air molecules would deflect the electrons. Glass lenses do not help with electrons. Instead, **magnetic fields** from **coils** with a current running through them focus the beam. They act as electromagnetic lenses. The image appears on a fluorescent screen or a sensor.

In a **transmission electron microscope** (TEM), the electrons pass through wafer-thin slices. Biological samples are often given contrast with **heavy-metal salts** such as uranyl acetate, which make structures show up dark. The **scanning electron microscope** (SEM), on the other hand, scans surfaces with a fine beam. It produces images that look three-dimensional, for example of the head of a fly. In **freeze-fracture**, flash-frozen samples are split open to show the inside of membranes.

The German physicist **Ernst Ruska** developed the first electron microscope from 1931 with **Max Knoll** at the Technical University of Berlin. It was not until **1986** that Ruska received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it. The Swiss biophysicist **Jacques Dubochet** of the **University of Lausanne** was honoured with the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in **2017**. He shared it with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.

Dubochet found a way of freezing samples in a flash in **glass-like ice**. No ice crystals form that would destroy the sample. This makes it possible to look at proteins and viruses in their natural state. This **cryo-electron microscopy** now helps, for example, in developing medicines.

gewusst: More than 50 years lay between the building of the first electron microscope and Ruska's Nobel Prize.
Modern electron microscopes can even make single atoms visible.

teile.einleitung: An echo is a sound that bounces off a hard surface and comes back to us. In the mountains, this is how you hear your own shout a second time.
wichtigste: An echo happens when sound bounces off a hard wall.
The wall has to be far enough away for you to hear the shout separately.
Sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air.
In Switzerland, you can often hear an echo in the mountains.
Bats and dolphins find their way using echoes.
The name comes from the nymph Echo in a Greek legend.

abschnitte.text: If you shout across to a **rock face**, the shout comes back. The **sound** bounces off the hard surface like a ball off a wall. That is why you often hear an echo in the **Alps**. But the wall has to be **far enough away**. If it is too close, the sound comes back so quickly that it blends with your own shout.

Sound is fast, but not infinitely fast. In air it travels about **340 metres per second**. That is faster than a passenger plane, but much slower than light. The sound has to travel to the wall and back again. That is why you hear the echo **a little later** than your own shout. If the wall is 170 metres away, it takes about one second.

In an **empty gym**, the sound bounces off the hard walls, the floor and the ceiling. It rings out, almost like an echo. **Soft things** such as curtains, carpets or cushions swallow the sound. That is why an empty room sounds much louder than a furnished one.

**Bats** call out very high sounds that we cannot hear. From the echoes, they can tell where **obstacles** and **insects** are, even in the dark. This is called **echolocation**. **Dolphins** also use echoes: they send out clicking sounds and so recognise fish and rocks. Ships do something similar: with an **echo sounder**, they measure how deep the water is.

The word comes from a **Greek legend**. In it, the **nymph Echo** could no longer speak for herself, but could only repeat the last words of others. The echo is named after her, because an echo also only repeats what we shout.

gewusst: In water, sound travels more than four times as fast as in air.
Some rocks and valleys in the Alps are known among hikers for their especially good echo.

teile.einleitung: Edward Jenner was an English country doctor. In 1796 he carried out the first scientifically tested vaccination, against the dangerous disease smallpox. That is why he is often called the father of vaccination.
wichtigste: Edward Jenner was a country doctor from Berkeley in England.
He developed the first vaccine, against smallpox.
On 14 May 1796 he vaccinated a boy called James Phipps.
For this he used the harmless cowpox.
The word “vaccination” comes from the Latin “vacca”, meaning cow.
Jenner is regarded as the father of vaccination.

abschnitte.text: **Edward Jenner** lived from 1749 to 1823. He was a **country doctor** in **Berkeley** in the county of **Gloucestershire** in England. In his time, **smallpox** was one of the most feared diseases. Many people died of it, and survivors often had scars on their faces.

In the countryside it was well known that **milkmaids** who had caught the harmless **cowpox** did not catch real smallpox. In humans, cowpox is mild. Jenner took this observation seriously and wanted to **test it scientifically**. He suspected that cowpox prepares the body for the dangerous smallpox.

On **14 May 1796**, Jenner took material from a blister on a woman who had cowpox. He passed it on to eight-year-old **James Phipps**, the son of his gardener. It later turned out that the boy was **protected** against smallpox. Today, an experiment like this on a child would no longer be allowed, but back then these rules did not yet exist.

Jenner's method quickly spread all over **Europe**. The word **“vaccination”** reminds us of this: it comes from the Latin **“vacca”**, cow. Jenner's smallpox vaccine laid the foundation for all later **vaccines**. That is why he is often called the **father of vaccination**. Thanks to vaccinations around the world, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in **1980**.

gewusst: To this day, smallpox is the only human disease that has been completely wiped out.
The French scientist Louis Pasteur later suggested calling all vaccinations “vaccination” in honour of Jenner.

teile.einleitung: Electrolytes are substances that break up into electrically charged particles in water. In the body they are essential for nerves, muscles, the heart and the water balance.
wichtigste: An electrolyte breaks up into ions in solution and then conducts electricity.
Outside the cells, sodium is the most common positive ion.
Inside the cells, potassium is the most common positive ion.
Chloride is the most important negative ion outside the cells.
In the blood, normal levels are about 135 to 145 mmol/l of sodium and 3.5 to 5 mmol/l of potassium.
The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 sodium ions out and 2 potassium ions in.
About 99 per cent of the calcium is stored in the skeleton.

abschnitte.text: If you dissolve **table salt** in water, it breaks up into charged particles, the **ions**. Positively charged ones are called **cations**, negatively charged ones **anions**. Such substances are called **electrolytes**. Their solutions conduct electric current. In the body, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride and bicarbonate are especially important.

Outside the cells, **sodium** is the most common cation. It largely decides how much water is held there. In the blood, it is normally about **135 to 145 mmol/l** and is controlled very tightly. Deviations can affect the brain. **Chloride** accompanies sodium as its counter-ion and is about 100 mmol/l in plasma, and bicarbonate is about 24 mmol/l.

Inside the cells, **potassium** is the most common cation. There its concentration is about 30 times higher than in the blood. This is important for the **resting membrane potential**, the electrical voltage at the cell wall. In the blood, potassium is normally **3.5 to 5 mmol/l**. Even small deviations can disturb the **heart rhythm**.

To keep these differences in place, the **sodium-potassium pump** works in every cell. In each cycle it uses up one **ATP**, the cell's energy carrier. In doing so it moves **three sodium ions** out and **two potassium ions** in. A large part of the energy the body needs at rest goes into these pumps.

About **99 per cent** of the **calcium** is in bones and teeth as hydroxyapatite. The small remainder in the blood is essential for blood clotting, muscles and nerves. When there are disturbances, doctors have to be careful: if a long-standing, severe sodium deficiency is corrected too quickly, brain cells suddenly lose water. This can damage the protective sheaths of the nerve fibres.

gewusst: When you sweat, you lose not only water but also electrolytes, mainly sodium.
The term electrolyte goes back to the English scientist Michael Faraday.

teile.einleitung: An electrocardiogram, ECG for short, records the electrical activity of the heart. Electrodes on the skin measure tiny voltages that arise with every heartbeat.
wichtigste: An ECG measures electrical voltages on the skin in the millivolt range.
The P wave shows the excitation of the atria.
The QRS complex shows the excitation of the ventricles.
The T wave shows the excitation fading in the ventricles.
A standard resting ECG has 12 leads.
Willem Einthoven received the Nobel Prize in 1924 for the ECG.
ST segment elevation is a typical sign of a heart attack.

abschnitte.text: Before the heart muscle contracts, it is excited electrically. This **excitation** produces electric fields in the body. **Electrodes** on the skin measure the resulting voltage differences in the **millivolt** range. A machine records them as a curve. In this way you can see how the excitation travels through the heart.

The **P wave** appears when the excitation spreads from the **sinus node** across both atria. The large **QRS complex** shows the excitation of the ventricles. The **T wave** shows how the excitation fades again in the ventricles. The fading in the atria cannot be seen, because it happens at the same time as the much larger QRS complex. The **PQ interval** measures the conduction from the atria to the ventricles, and the normal range is 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.

ECG paper usually runs at 25 millimetres per second. If two R spikes are 20 millimetres apart, one beat lasts 0.8 seconds. 60 seconds divided by 0.8 gives **75 beats per minute**. A **standard resting ECG** has **12 leads**: 6 on the arms and legs and 6 on the chest wall, called V1 to V6.

The Dutch physiologist **Willem Einthoven** developed the string galvanometer, a very sensitive measuring device. With it he created the modern ECG. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in **1924**. The names P, Q, R, S and T for the waves also go back to him.

The ECG is used to detect heart rhythm disorders and other heart problems. A typical sign of an acute **heart attack** is **ST segment elevation**. This is then called a STEMI. Rescue services in Switzerland therefore have ECG machines in their vehicles.

gewusst: The first ECG machines weighed several hundred kilograms, and the patients put their hands and feet into basins of salt water.
Today some smartwatches can record a simple ECG.

teile.einleitung: For many people, showering is part of their daily washing routine. You wash off sweat and dirt and feel fresh afterwards. With a few tricks, you can also save water.
wichtigste: A short shower usually uses less water than a bath.
After sport, you wash off the sweat.
Before swimming in an indoor pool, you have to shower.
You can turn the water off while you soap yourself.
The shower water should be pleasantly warm, not too hot.
A rubber mat protects against slipping.

abschnitte.text: When playing and doing **sport**, you sweat. If the **sweat** stays on your skin, it soon starts to smell, because bacteria break it down. Showering washes off sweat and dirt. For washing you use **shower gel**, a liquid soap for the skin. Washing-up liquid, on the other hand, is meant for dishes. The water comes out of the **shower head**, which has many small holes.

At an **indoor pool**, you shower **before swimming**. This keeps sweat, skin cream and dirt out of the pool water, and the water stays cleaner. The pool water contains **chlorine**, which kills germs but can dry out the skin. That is why you also shower **after swimming**, to rinse off the chlorinated water.

The water should be **pleasantly warm**. **Water that is too hot** can scald the skin and dries it out. Wet tiles are very **slippery**. That is why many showers have a **rubber mat** with little bumps, so that you stand safely. After showering, you dry yourself well, also between the toes.

A full **bath** needs a lot of water. A **short shower** usually needs much less. You save even more if you **turn the water off** while you soap yourself. Because warm water first has to be heated, showering for less time also saves **energy**. A water-saving shower head helps as well.

gewusst: A water-saving shower head mixes air into the water, so that less water flows through and it still feels powerful.
Showering too often or for a very long time can dry out the skin.

teile.einleitung: Loneliness is the distressing feeling of having too few real relationships with other people. It can affect anyone, older people just as much as teenagers.
wichtigste: Being alone can be pleasant, but loneliness is a painful feeling.
Social isolation means that someone really has hardly any contacts.
Loneliness that lasts a long time acts like constant stress and can harm health.
Besides older people, many young adults also feel lonely.
Clubs, groups and hobbies help you find new contacts.
Online contacts do not fully replace real meetings.

abschnitte.text: Many people like being **alone** from time to time, for example when reading or hiking. They still feel connected with others. **Loneliness** is something different: you feel misunderstood or have too few close relationships. You can even feel lonely in the middle of a group. When someone objectively has hardly any contacts, this is called **social isolation**.

Almost everyone knows short phases of loneliness. If it lasts a long time, it means lasting **stress** for the body. Studies show links with **cardiovascular diseases** and **depression**. That is why loneliness is now seen as an important health issue. It is worth taking seriously.

In January 2018, the politician Tracey Crouch was given responsibility for the issue of loneliness in **Great Britain**. In this way loneliness was recognised as a problem for society. In Switzerland, too, it is being researched and discussed. Surveys show that besides older people, many **teenagers and young adults** also feel lonely.

Someone who feels lonely can join a **club**, a sports group or a course. There you meet people with the same interests. Volunteering also brings contacts. **Social media** can connect people, but does not replace meeting in person. Someone who keeps comparing themselves with others can even feel lonelier. Talking with people you trust or with advice centres also helps.

If a classmate often stands alone at break, a small step can make a big difference: **speak to them and invite them**. Often the person is just waiting for it. A friendly question or a game together can be the start of a friendship.

gewusst: In 2018, Great Britain was one of the first countries to give a member of the government responsibility for the issue of loneliness.
You can feel lonely in the middle of many people and be happy on your own.

teile.einleitung: Jealousy is a strong feeling that almost everyone knows. You are afraid that someone else will be favoured and that you will get less love or attention yourself.
wichtigste: Jealousy is the fear of being noticed or loved less than someone else.
Almost everyone feels jealous at some point, it is a normal feeling.
Jealousy is common between brothers and sisters, for example when a baby needs a lot of care.
Jealous children often want to show: I am still here too.
Talking about your own feelings helps most.
Being generous means being happy for others, it is the opposite of envy.

abschnitte.text: Someone who is jealous fears losing something important: a person's love, friendship or attention. Jealousy often comes together with anger, sadness or fear. Closely related is **envy**. You are envious when someone else has something you would like to have yourself. For strong envy there is the saying “green with envy”.

When a new **baby brother or sister** is born, the baby needs a lot of care. The parents then have less time for the older children. These children sometimes feel pushed aside and become jealous. Some children then behave like a baby again or get up to mischief. Behind this there is usually a wish for **attention**. Jealousy can also arise between older siblings or between friends.

Researchers have studied how **dogs** react when their human strokes a toy dog. Many dogs pushed in between and shoved the toy dog away. This suggests that dogs, too, can feel a kind of jealousy. Anyone with several pets often notices that they compete for cuddles.

Jealousy is unpleasant, but no reason to feel ashamed. What helps best is to **say how you feel**. If you talk about your feelings, you can find a solution together with others. Parents can, for example, deliberately spend time alone with each child. It is also important not to take anything away from others and not to hurt anyone.

The opposite of envy is **being generous**. Someone who is generous is happy for others when they get something nice or are good at something. This does not always work straight away. It helps to think about the good things you have yourself. If you are happy for others, you make others and yourself happy.

gewusst: The saying “green with envy” has been around for a very long time, and in English too, envy is described as being green.
In one study, jealous dogs pushed away a toy dog that their human was stroking.

teile.einleitung: Pus is a thick, usually yellowish liquid that forms in some inflammations. It shows that the body is fighting hard against bacteria.
wichtigste: Pus consists of dead defence cells, germs and broken-down tissue.
Pus is usually yellowish to greenish and cloudy.
Common germs that cause pus are staphylococci.
An abscess is a pocket of pus in tissue that has newly broken down.
An empyema is pus in a body cavity that already exists.
A boil is a pus-filled inflammation of a hair follicle.
A pustule is a small blister of pus on the skin.

abschnitte.text: When bacteria get into the body, it sends **white blood cells** to defend it. Many of these defence cells die in the fight. Together with the germs and broken-down tissue, they form a thick liquid, **pus**. Pus is especially often caused by **staphylococci**. The most important germ in skin and wound infections with pus is Staphylococcus aureus.

Pus is usually **yellowish** to greenish and cloudy. The colour comes from the many cells. Certain white blood cells, the **neutrophil granulocytes**, contain the greenish enzyme **myeloperoxidase**. It helps to kill bacteria and turns the pus greenish.

An **abscess** is a walled-off collection of pus. Tissue breaks down, and a new cavity full of pus forms. In an **empyema**, on the other hand, pus collects in a body cavity that already exists, for example in a sinus or in the space around the lungs. Both often need medical treatment, and sometimes the pus is drained.

A **pustule** is a small blister of pus, as found for example in acne. A **papule**, on the other hand, is a small bump without pus. A **boil** forms when bacteria get into a hair follicle. A painful lump full of pus develops. You should not squeeze such spots, because the inflammation could otherwise spread.

gewusst: In the past, doctors often thought pus in wounds was a good sign of healing.
The word staphylococci comes from Greek and means roughly “little grape-like balls”, because under the microscope they look like bunches of grapes.

teile.einleitung: The vaccination rate, also called vaccination coverage, shows what percentage of a group has been vaccinated against a particular disease. It shows how well a population is protected against infectious diseases.
wichtigste: The vaccination rate is the share of a group that has received a particular vaccination.
For measles, the WHO recommends a rate of 95 per cent with two doses.
Switzerland measures vaccination coverage among 2-, 8- and 16-year-olds.
The entries in the vaccination record are what gets counted.
High rates also protect people who cannot be vaccinated.
Local gaps in vaccination can still lead to outbreaks.

abschnitte.text: The **vaccination rate** tells you what percentage of a group has received a particular vaccination. It is often measured separately by **age** and **vaccine dose**. Here is an example: at a school, 552 out of 600 teenagers have had two measles vaccinations. 552 divided by 600 gives 0.92. So the vaccination rate is **92 per cent**.

The Swiss **vaccination coverage monitoring** regularly examines the vaccination records of **2-, 8- and 16-year-olds** in the **cantons**. What is counted are the vaccinations and doses written down in the **vaccination record**, not the antibodies measured in the blood. The results are published by the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH). This shows where there are still gaps.

If almost everyone is immune, a germ rarely meets anyone it can infect. **Chains of infection** break. This also protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as **babies** or people with a weakened immune system. This is called **herd protection**. Because measles is extremely contagious, the WHO says at least **95 per cent** of people need to be immune for this to work.

abschnitte.titel: Vaccinated does not always mean protected
abschnitte.text: No vaccine works for everyone who is vaccinated. Here is a calculation: in a municipality, **85 per cent** of the children are vaccinated, and the vaccine works for **95 per cent** of them. The protected share is then 0.85 times 0.95, which is 0.8075. That is **about 81 per cent** of all children. This is why a high vaccination rate is needed to get enough protection.

Even when the rate is high across the whole country, **measles outbreaks** can happen. Averages hide **local gaps in vaccination**. Where unvaccinated people are grouped together, for example in certain regions, schools or communities, the virus can still spread.

gewusst: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known.
In Switzerland, you can have your vaccination record checked at a pharmacy or by a doctor.

teile.einleitung: Iron is a trace element that the body needs only in small amounts, but it is essential. It is found mainly in the red pigment of the blood and helps to carry oxygen.
wichtigste: An adult has only about 3 to 5 grams of iron in the body.
Most of it is in the red blood pigment haemoglobin.
A serious lack of iron can lead to anaemia.
Iron is stored in the protein ferritin.
Vitamin C improves the absorption of iron from plants.
Black tea with a meal can reduce absorption.
Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum.

abschnitte.text: Iron is an important building block of **haemoglobin**, the red blood pigment. In the lungs, haemoglobin binds oxygen and carries it to all the cells. An adult has only about **3 to 5 grams** of iron, roughly as much as in a small nail. Even so, the body cannot do without it. It is also needed in muscles and in some enzymes.

Iron from food is absorbed mainly in the **duodenum**, the first part of the small intestine. The body absorbs only a small part of the iron in food. It is stored in the protein **ferritin**, mainly in the liver, spleen and bone marrow. A low ferritin level in the blood shows that the iron stores are empty.

If iron is missing, the body cannot make enough haemoglobin. This leads to **iron-deficiency anaemia**. People affected are often tired, pale and less able to perform. Iron deficiency is one of the most common nutrient deficiencies in the world. A doctor can check with a blood test whether someone has too little iron.

Iron is found in meat, but also in many foods from plants. Good sources are **pulses** such as lentils, as well as wholegrain foods, nuts and seeds. Cucumbers and apples, on the other hand, contain little iron. **Vitamin C** helps the gut absorb iron from plants better. A glass of orange juice with lentils therefore makes sense.

Some substances make it harder to absorb iron. The **tannins** in **black tea** bind iron in the gut. That is why it is better not to drink tea straight with iron-rich meals, but a little later. Coffee can also reduce absorption.

gewusst: The iron in blood is what makes blood red.
The body can hardly get rid of iron actively, and it controls the amount mainly through absorption in the gut.

teile.einleitung: Disgust is a strong feeling that warns us about harmful things. When you feel disgusted, you want to get rid of something at once or not touch it at all.
wichtigste: Disgust protects against spoiled food that could make you ill.
When disgusted, people often say “Yuck” or “Ugh”.
Something disgusting in the mouth is usually spat out at once.
Strong disgust can lead to feeling sick and retching.
The nose often warns about spoiled food first.
Since 2017, some insects have been allowed as food in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Disgust** is one of the basic human feelings. It stops us from eating things that could make us ill. A typical sign is a twisted face with a wrinkled nose. People then say “**Yuck**” or “**Ugh**”. With strong disgust you can feel **sick**, and sometimes you even have to retch.

Spoiled food smells bad. That is why you often notice it first with your **nose**. Taste also warns you: if something tastes odd, you usually **spit** it out straight away. This stops inedible things from reaching the stomach. So disgust is a kind of shield for the body.

Most people feel disgusted by **mould**. Mould grows as a furry, fluffy coating, often green, white or black. Some moulds produce poisons. That is why you do not eat mouldy bread any more, not even if you only cut off the spot. Here, disgust protects us sensibly.

What disgusts you also depends on what you are used to. In many countries, people have eaten **insects** for a long time. In **Switzerland**, mealworms, crickets and migratory locusts have been allowed to be sold as food since **2017**. Even so, many people still find them disgusting. What counts as a delicacy in one country is disgusting to others.

gewusst: Small children hardly feel disgust yet, and they learn a lot of it only over time.
In 2017, Switzerland was one of the first countries in Europe to expressly allow insects as food.

teile.einleitung: The ellipsoid joint is a special type of joint in our body. It is also known as the egg joint because its joint head is elongated like an egg and sits in an oval socket.
wichtigste: In an ellipsoid joint, an egg-shaped joint head sits in an oval socket.
An ellipsoid joint allows movements around two axes.
Turning around its own axis is not possible.
Another name is the egg joint.
The joint between the radius and the wrist bones is an ellipsoid joint.
The upper joint of the head, between the skull and the first neck vertebra, is also an ellipsoid joint.

abschnitte.text: A joint connects two bones so that they can move. In an ellipsoid joint, the **joint head** is long and rounded, like an egg. It fits into an equally long **joint socket**. An ellipse is an oval, which is why the egg joint is also called an **ellipsoid joint**. The shape of a joint decides which movements are possible.

An ellipsoid joint allows movements around **two axes**. So you can move it forwards and backwards and to the side. Turning around its own axis, however, is not possible. The oval head only fits into the long socket in one position. If you turned it, it would jam and knock against the edge. A ball-and-socket joint such as the shoulder, on the other hand, can move in all directions.

The best-known ellipsoid joint is the **proximal wrist joint**. It connects the **radius** with the wrist bones. Three bones of the first row of wrist bones together form the egg-shaped head: the **scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum**. The socket is formed by the radius and a disc of cartilage. With this joint you can bend the hand up and down and tilt it towards the thumb side or the little-finger side.

abschnitte.titel: The upper joint of the head
abschnitte.text: There is also an ellipsoid joint between the head and the spine. The **upper joint of the head** connects the occipital bone of the skull with the first neck vertebra, the **atlas**. It is a paired joint, so there is one on the left and one on the right. With it you can mainly nod. Turning the head is done by another joint further down.

gewusst: The first neck vertebra is called the atlas, after a figure from Greek legend who carries the vault of the heavens.
The fact that the hand can still be turned is not due to the wrist joint, but to the radius rotating around the ulna in the forearm.

teile.einleitung: When we breathe in, we bring fresh air into the lungs. The most important helper is a muscle you cannot see: the diaphragm.
wichtigste: When you breathe in, the lungs fill with air.
The diaphragm below the lungs is the most important breathing muscle.
The lungs sit in the chest and are protected by the ribs.
The left lung is smaller because the heart needs room there.
In the end, the air reaches tiny air sacs called alveoli.
We breathe in through the nose and mouth.

abschnitte.text: Air enters the body through the **nose** or the **mouth**. In the nose it is warmed, moistened and cleaned of dust. Then it flows through the throat into the **windpipe**. This divides into two branches, the bronchi. They branch out like a tree into ever finer tubes.

The **lungs** fill almost the whole **chest**. The ribs protect them on all sides. They consist of two lobes. The left one is slightly smaller, because the **heart** lies more on the left side and needs room. At the end of the finest tubes sit millions of tiny **alveoli**. This is where the blood takes up oxygen.

The **diaphragm** is a flat, dome-shaped muscle below the lungs. When you breathe in, it tightens and becomes flatter. This makes more room in the chest, and air flows in. Muscles between the ribs also help by lifting the chest. When you breathe out, the muscles relax and the air flows out again.

Put one hand on your tummy and breathe in deeply. You can feel your **tummy bulge outwards**. The diaphragm lowers and pushes the organs of the abdomen down and forwards. This is called **abdominal breathing**. Calm, deep breathing can help you relax.

gewusst: At rest, a person breathes in about 12 to 20 times a minute.
The surface of all the alveoli together is roughly as big as half a tennis court.

teile.einleitung: Electroencephalography, EEG for short, measures the electrical activity of the brain. For this, electrodes are stuck to the scalp, and the brain currents are recorded as wavy lines.
wichtigste: Hans Berger recorded the first EEG of a human in Jena in 1924.
The signals at the scalp are only a few microvolts strong.
Alpha waves show relaxed wakefulness with the eyes closed.
Beta waves appear during concentrated activity.
Delta waves below 4 Hz are typical of deep sleep.
The electrodes are arranged according to the 10-20 system.
The EEG is especially important for diagnosing epilepsy.

abschnitte.text: In 1924, the German psychiatrist **Hans Berger** recorded the brain currents of a human for the first time, in **Jena**. He published his results in 1929 and introduced the name **electroencephalogram**. The word comes from Greek: “enkephalos” means brain, “graphein” means to write. Today the EEG is a standard test in hospitals.

Nerve cells work with small electric currents. The EEG signal comes mainly from the **pyramidal cells** of the cerebral cortex. Many of these cells, lined up in parallel, produce currents at their contact points at the same time. Their sum can be measured at the scalp. The signals are only a few to about a hundred **microvolts** strong, so sensitive amplifiers are needed.

Depending on the state, the EEG shows different waves. **Alpha waves** of about 8 to 13 Hz appear in calm wakefulness with the eyes closed. When you open your eyes, they become weaker. **Beta waves** of about 13 to 30 Hz show an active, alert brain. **Delta waves** below 4 Hz are slow and tall and mark **deep sleep**.

For an EEG, electrodes are placed on the scalp, often with a cap. Their positions follow the international **10-20 system**. The electrodes lie at distances of 10 or 20 per cent of certain lines across the head. This makes measurements comparable for different head sizes. The test does not hurt.

abschnitte.titel: What the EEG is needed for
abschnitte.text: The EEG is especially important in **epilepsy**. There it often shows typical spikes and steep waves. This makes it possible to work out the type of seizure and the place in the brain where the seizures start. The EEG also helps in **sleep medicine** and in cases of unconsciousness.

gewusst: Hans Berger worked on his method for years before he published it.
The brain is never completely silent even in sleep, and the EEG then simply shows other waves.

teile.einleitung: Iron deficiency means that the body has too little iron. You need iron mainly to make haemoglobin, the red blood pigment. If it is missing, you often feel weak and tired.
wichtigste: Iron is a trace element that the body has to take in with food.
The body needs iron mainly to make haemoglobin.
Haemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood.
Iron deficiency is the most common nutrient deficiency in the world.
Typical signs are tiredness, paleness and problems concentrating.
Meat, pulses and wholegrain foods provide iron.
Vitamin C helps you absorb iron from plant foods.

abschnitte.text: Iron is a **trace element** that the body needs only in small amounts. An adult has only about 3 to 5 grams of iron in the whole body. If you get too little over a longer time, the iron stores run empty. This is called **iron deficiency**.

abschnitte.titel: What does the body need iron for?
abschnitte.text: Most of the iron is in the **haemoglobin** of the red blood cells. Haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and carries it to all parts of the body. Muscles and many enzymes also need iron. Without enough iron, the cells get too little oxygen.

Typical signs are tiredness, paleness and reduced performance. Some people have brittle nails, hair loss or cracked corners of the mouth. If the deficiency is severe, it leads to **anaemia**. Only a blood test can show whether there is an iron deficiency.

Girls and women are especially often affected, because they lose iron during their monthly period. Teenagers who are growing and pregnant women also need more iron. People who eat a vegetarian or vegan diet should pay attention to iron-rich foods. Endurance athletes can also have a higher need.

A lot of iron that the body can use well is found in **meat** and fish. Plant sources are lentils, beans, oat flakes, millet, nuts and pumpkin seeds. A glass of orange juice or some pepper with the meal improves absorption, because vitamin C helps. Black tea and coffee with the meal slow it down.

If a deficiency is found, the doctor often prescribes **iron tablets**. In severe cases, iron can also be given through a drip. In Switzerland, iron infusions are used fairly often. You should only take iron supplements on a doctor's advice, because too much iron is also harmful.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mineral that the body needs only in very small amounts.
The red blood pigment that carries oxygen.
A lack of red blood pigment in the blood.
A storage protein for iron, whose level can be measured in the blood.

gewusst: Spinach contains less iron than was long claimed, and the body can absorb it from spinach only poorly.
Iron in the blood is the reason why blood tastes slightly metallic.
According to the World Health Organization, hundreds of millions of people around the world are affected by anaemia.

teile.einleitung: A bedtime routine is a fixed sequence of steps before sleeping that is the same every evening. It helps the body become calm and fall asleep more easily.
wichtigste: You do a bedtime routine the same way every evening.
This lets the body notice that bedtime is coming soon.
Brushing your teeth is part of it every evening.
A calm bedtime story relaxes you, while wild games keep you awake.
Fixed bedtimes help the body clock.
A lullaby is a calm song for falling asleep.

abschnitte.text: A **routine** is something you always do the same way. If you repeat the same steps every evening, the body gets used to it. It then knows: soon it will be time to sleep. Fixed **bedtimes** also help. The **body clock** then makes sure you get tired at the right time every evening.

Before sleeping you brush your **teeth**, so that they stay clean overnight. Many people then put on their pyjamas and go to the toilet once more. After that comes something calm, for example a **bedtime story**. At the end you say “Good night” to each other. What matters is that the sequence is similar every evening.

A **lullaby** is a calm song for falling asleep. In the past it was sung while rocking the baby in the cradle. A well-known one is, for example, “Weisst du, wie viel Sternlein stehen” (“Do you know how many little stars there are”). Reading aloud or listening to a story is also relaxing. Exciting films and wild games, on the other hand, tend to keep you awake.

An old tip is **counting sheep**. Counting evenly is boring and is supposed to make you tired. A glass of **warm milk** suits the evening well, because it contains no **caffeine**. Drinks with caffeine, such as cola or black tea, can keep you awake. Screens just before bedtime also often make it harder to fall asleep.

gewusst: The German word for lullaby, Wiegenlied, comes from Wiege, a rocking baby's cot.
Many adults also have bedtime routines, for example reading a few pages.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Commission for Vaccination, FCV for short, advises the Confederation on all questions about vaccinations. Together with the Federal Office of Public Health, it draws up the vaccination recommendations for Switzerland.
wichtigste: The FCV is an extra-parliamentary commission of the Confederation.
Its members are chosen by the Federal Council.
It draws up vaccination recommendations and advises the FOPH and the Federal Council.
It is not the FCV but Swissmedic that may approve vaccines.
Recommended vaccinations are mostly paid for by basic health insurance.
In Germany, the STIKO has a similar role.

abschnitte.text: The FCV is an **extra-parliamentary commission**. Commissions of this kind advise the **Federal Council** and the **federal administration** with expert knowledge from outside. The FCV is appointed by the Federal Council, and its members are **experts** from medicine and healthcare. It deals with all questions about vaccinations.

The FCV assesses **scientific data** and, together with the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH), draws up **vaccination recommendations**. In doing so it weighs up how common and how serious a disease is, that is, the **disease burden**. It also checks how well and how safely a vaccine works, whether the vaccination can be put into practice and what it costs. The recommendations are set out in the **Swiss vaccination schedule**.

Whether a vaccine may be sold at all is decided not by the FCV but by **Swissmedic**. This authority checks **quality, safety and effectiveness** and grants the **approval**. Only after that does the question arise of whether, and for whom, a vaccination is recommended. That is the work of the FCV and the FOPH.

For many **recommended vaccinations**, the **compulsory health insurance**, the basic insurance, covers the costs. The condition is that they are listed in the **Health Insurance Benefits Ordinance**. **Travel vaccinations** are mostly not covered. So the FCV's recommendations also affect what families have to pay for themselves.

Other countries also have expert bodies like this. In **Germany**, the **Standing Committee on Vaccination** (STIKO) at the Robert Koch Institute publishes the vaccination recommendations. In the **USA**, the **Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices** (ACIP) advises the health authority CDC. There, approval is granted by the **FDA**, much like Swissmedic in Switzerland.

gewusst: The Swiss vaccination schedule is revised regularly when new scientific findings become available.
A vaccination recommendation is not compulsory: in Switzerland, people usually decide for themselves whether to be vaccinated.

teile.einleitung: Thirst is the feeling that tells us: the body needs water. Because we lose water every day, we also have to drink every day.
wichtigste: More than half of the body is made of water.
We lose water when we sweat, breathe and go to the toilet.
On hot days and during sport, you need to drink especially much.
Pale yellow urine usually shows that you are drinking enough.
If you drink too little, you get tired and may get a headache.
A person can only survive a few days without water.

abschnitte.text: The human body is made of **more than half water**. In children the share is slightly higher than in older people. Water carries nutrients in the blood, helps with digestion and cools the body. A person can last a long time without food, but **only a few days** without drinking.

The body gives off water when we **sweat**, **breathe** and go to the **toilet**. That is why you have to drink every day. On **hot days** and during **sport** you sweat especially much. Then the body needs more water. The brain notices when water is missing and speaks up with the feeling of **thirst**.

**Water** quenches thirst best. In Switzerland, **tap water** is clean drinking water and is checked regularly. In many towns and cities there are also fountains with drinking water. **Sugary drinks**, on the other hand, contain a lot of **sugar**. That harms the teeth, and they are less good at stopping thirst than water.

The colour of your urine often shows whether you are drinking enough. If it is **pale yellow**, everything is usually fine. If it is **dark yellow**, you should drink more. If you drink too little, you get **tired** and may get a **headache**. Thinking and concentrating also become harder. That is why a water bottle at school is a good idea.

gewusst: Fruit and vegetables such as cucumbers or melons are also mostly made of water.
If you feel thirsty, you have often already gone a little too long without drinking.
